The static lints

Source: vignettes/lints.Rmd
lints.Rmd

This article is for authors who want to find problems in a project’s documents without rendering them: numbers typed into the prose, constructs that will not parse, broken cross-references, figures without alt text. After it you will be able to run the lints, read their findings, fix or exempt each one, and tune the rules for a project.

library(weft)

What a lint is

A lint is a rule with a stable id. lints() reads every .qmd and .Rmd in a project as text, runs nothing, and returns the findings: one row for each place a rule matched, with its file, line and column, the rule, a message that ends with the rule’s number in the design, and a hint.

Every rule has a tier:

Tier What it is What happens
1 a hard rule, decidable from the source fails the commit, the render or verify()
2 a heuristic listed for newly added lines by changes() and verify(); blocks nothing
3 a human read the ranked list of changes(); never decided by weft

lint_rules() lists every rule:

lint_rules()[, c("id", "tier", "scope", "what")]
#>                id tier   scope                                                                what
#> 1         numeral    1    file A number typed in prose, a caption, front matter, a string or math.
#> 2       construct    1    file                          An error the scanner finds in a construct.
#> 3            read    1    file                                           A file that is not UTF-8.
#> 4     block-start    1    file                           A line inside a span that starts a block.
#> 5        lone-bar    2    file                             A bracket with one `|` and no governor.
#> 6         if-zero    2    file                             An `if` condition that compares with 0.
#> 7            name    2    file          A class or key that is not weft's, or is one edit from it.
#> 8     inert-check    1    file                        A check or condition with no variable in it.
#> 9      long-guard    2    file                              An `if` arm longer than `guard_words`.
#> 10       cite-key    1    file                       A key of a cite span not in the bibliography.
#> 11      cite-bare    1    file             A bare cite key not written as a citation in its block.
#> 12   citation-key    1    file                             A citation key not in the bibliography.
#> 13     claim-word    2    file                                         A claim word in a sentence.
#> 14  literal-value    1    file                                     A value made only of constants.
#> 15 value-constant    2    file                                  A numeric constant inside a value.
#> 16   value-format    2    file                             A value that rounds or formats in code.
#> 17           xref    1 project                                     A cross-reference to no anchor.
#> 18   anchor-twice    1 project                                   An anchor defined more than once.
#> 19      ref-label    1    file                  A span whose text is a reference-definition label.
#> 20  anchor-unused    2 project                A figure, table or equation anchor nobody refers to.
#> 21      xref-code    2    file                       A cross-reference written inside a code span.
#> 22 section-anchor    1    file                                          A heading with no `{#id}`.
#> 23    chunk-label    1    file                                    An executed chunk with no label.
#> 24       tar-name    1    file                         A target read that the store does not hold.
#> 25    dict-assign    1    file                                            An assignment to `dict`.
#> 26      file-link    1    file                        A link or image to a file that is not there.
#> 27    above-setup    1    file                A construct above the chunk that calls weft_setup().
#> 28       dict-key    1    file                       A `dict$key` read of a key that is not there.
#> 29      tar-cache    1    file                             A chunk that reads a target and caches.
#> 30   config-place    1 project             A project setting in a place that is not the project's.
#> 31         engine    1 project                     A document with constructs that is not knitr's.
#> 32         figure    1    file                        A figure with no label, caption or alt text.
#> 33  table-caption    1    file                                            A table with no caption.
#> 34   guest-inline    1    file          Inline code in another language, which knitr does not run.
#> 35     guest-call    1    file                    A weft function called from Python through `r.`.
#> 36     guest-read    2    file         A value read from Python or Julia that weft does not check.
#> 37      ojs-value    2    file               An Observable value computed in the reader's browser.

A rule’s scope is file when it reads one document at a time, and project when it reads them all, as cross-references do.

Running the lints

This project has an empty _weft.yml and one document with several problems:

writeLines("", "_weft.yml")
writeLines(c(
  "---",
  "title: \"Survey\"",
  "---",
  "",
  "## Results {#sec-results}",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "#| label: data",
  "n_sites <- 12",
  "```",
  "",
  "We visited 14 sites in 2023, and Site 4 was dry.",
  "Of these, `r 3 + 4` were above the trigger.",
  "Turbidity [rose | fell]{if=\"slope > 0\" .num}.",
  "All sites were sampled at `r n_sites` locations.",
  "Samples were filtered through [0.45 µm]{.weft-literal why=\"pore size set by the laboratory method\"} membranes.",
  "Discharge [rose | fell]{iff=\"q > 0\"} after the storm.",
  "See Figure 2 for the map.",
  "",
  "## Methods",
  "",
  "```{r}",
  "plot(1:3)",
  "```"
), "survey.qmd")
lints()
#> weft lints: 9 findings in 1 file (9 tier 1, 0 tier 2)
#> 
#> survey.qmd
#>   1:1    engine          survey.qmd holds weft constructs but is not marked `engine: knitr` and no document includes it (rule 5.8.9).
#>                          Add `engine: knitr` to its front matter.
#>   12:12  numeral         "14" is a number typed in prose (rule 5.2.1).
#>                          Write it as a value, put it in the dictionary, or mark it [14]{.weft-literal why="..."}.
#>   12:24  numeral         "2023" is a number typed in prose (rule 5.2.1).
#>                          Write it as a value, put it in the dictionary, or mark it [2023]{.weft-literal why="..."}.
#>   12:39  numeral         "4" is a number typed in prose (rule 5.2.1).
#>                          Write it as a value, put it in the dictionary, or mark it [4]{.weft-literal why="..."}.
#>   13:14  literal-value   `3 + 4` is made only of constants, so it is a number typed in the source (rule 5.6.1).
#>                          Compute it, put it in the dictionary, or write [3 + 4]{.weft-literal why="..."}.
#>   14:11  construct       A formatter on an `if` span is an error (rule 1.5.7): .num.
#>   18:12  numeral         "2" after "Figure" is a typed cross-reference number; use @fig-<label> (rule 5.2.4).
#>                          Write @fig-<label> and give the target that label.
#>   20:4   section-anchor  The heading `Methods` has no `{#id}` (rule 5.8.1).
#>                          Give it an id, for example `{#sec-name}`.
#>   22:1   chunk-label     The r chunk `plot(1:3)` has no label (rule 5.8.1).
#>                          Give the chunk a label, as `#| label: name`.

By default lints() runs the tier-1 rules over the whole project. lints(files = ) limits the report to some documents, rules = names rules by id, and tier = 2 or tier = 1:2 asks for the heuristics:

lints(tier = 2)
#> weft lints: 5 findings in 1 file (0 tier 1, 5 tier 2)
#> 
#> survey.qmd
#>   14:29  if-zero     The condition `slope > 0` compares with 0, which is a threshold typed in the source (rule 5.3.3).
#>                      A comparison with zero probably wants `sign`: write [a | b | c]{sign="..."} with an arm for each of positive, negative and zero (rule 5.3.3).
#>   15:1   claim-word  Claim word "all" in a sentence with a value; check that the value still bears it out, or guard the word with an `if` span (rule 5.5.1).
#>                      "All sites were sampled at `r n_sites` locations."
#>   17:12  claim-word  Claim words "rose", "fell" in a sentence with no value: if it states a result, compute it (rule 5.5.1).
#>                      "Discharge [rose | fell]{iff="q > 0"} after the storm."
#>   17:12  lone-bar    The bracket `[rose | fell]` holds one `|` and has no governor, so it is not read as arms (rule 5.3.3).
#>                      Add a governor (`n`, `if`, `sign`, `list`) or escape the bar as `\|`.
#>   17:25  name        `iff` is not a name weft knows; it is one edit from `if` (rule 5.3.3).
#>                      Check the spelling, or list the name under `expected_names` in _weft.yml.

Typed numbers

The rule numeral is the centre of the lints. Every numeral in the prose must be one of these:

  • a computed value, `r n_sites`;
  • a value from the dictionary, `r dict$trigger`;
  • inside a cite span, because it is quoted from a source;
  • inside a .weft-literal span or block, with a why that says why it is fixed.

A word whose first letter or digit is a digit is a numeral: “12”, “45%”, “11-year”, “3rd”, “1990s”. A word that starts with a letter is a name: “CO2”, “PM2.5”. The rule reads the body, captions, the front-matter fields that take constructs, weft_str() strings, and inline math, where an exponent or a subscript is exempt.

The .weft-literal span in the example above is why “0.45” is not a finding. Its why is the record: nothing else lists it.

Two settings in _weft.yml exempt more:

  • label_words: words after which a number is a name, not a quantity, such as “Site” in “Site 4”. The list starts empty. label_seed() proposes candidates from the prose.
  • numeral_years: true exempts a four-digit year from 1000 to 2999, a year range such as 2016-17, a decade and a possessive year. It is off by default, because a year in prose is often a choice that belongs in the dictionary.
label_seed(min_count = 1)
#>   word n files                 where
#> 1 Site 1     1 survey.qmd:12: Site 4
writeLines(c("label_words: [Site]", "numeral_years: true"), "_weft.yml")
lints(rules = "numeral")
#> weft lints: 2 findings in 1 file (2 tier 1, 0 tier 2)
#> 
#> survey.qmd
#>   12:12  numeral  "14" is a number typed in prose (rule 5.2.1).
#>                   Write it as a value, put it in the dictionary, or mark it [14]{.weft-literal why="..."}.
#>   18:12  numeral  "2" after "Figure" is a typed cross-reference number; use @fig-<label> (rule 5.2.4).
#>                   Write @fig-<label> and give the target that label.

A number after a word Quarto can cross-reference (“Figure 2”, “Table 3”, “Section 4”) is never exempt: write a cross-reference such as @fig-map instead.

When weft is adopted, a project’s existing documents may hold hundreds of typed numbers. The commit gate tolerates the ones already committed and refuses only new ones, so adoption can be gradual. See vignette("gate", package = "weft").

Literal values

A value made only of constants, such as `r 3 + 4` or {n="3"}, renders, but it is a number typed in the source. The rule literal-value finds it. Compute the number, put it in the dictionary, or write it as a .weft-literal with its why.

The tier-2 rules value-constant and value-format list a numeric constant inside a computation (other than 0 and 1) and a value that rounds in code with round(), format() or sprintf(). Rounding in code skips weft’s formatters, so the value has no printed record and round() drops trailing zeros.

Construct errors

A construct error is a mistake in weft syntax that the scanner finds without running R: a formatter on an if span, as in the example, the wrong number of arms, two classes from one group, a " inside an attribute value, an id defined twice. The rule is construct. A render stops at the first construct error, and the commit gate refuses a changed document that holds one, whatever HEAD held.

The rule block-start finds a line inside a span that Pandoc would read as the start of a new block, which cuts the span in two.

Checks that cannot fail

The rule inert-check finds a claim() check, or an if condition, with no variable in it: claim(x, TRUE) or if="1 > 0". Such a check cannot fail, and such a condition always chooses the same arm, so neither checks anything.

Cross-references, citations and figures

Rule Finds
xref a reference, such as @fig-map or a link to #sec-x, with no anchor anywhere in the project
anchor-twice an anchor defined twice
ref-label a span whose text is also a reference-link label in the document
cite-key, citation-key a citation key that is not in the bibliography
cite-bare a bare-form cite span whose key is not cited in the same block
figure a figure with no label, caption or alt text
table-caption a table with no caption
section-anchor a heading with no {#id}
chunk-label an executed chunk with no label

A missing section anchor or chunk label matters because the ledger keys each value on its section, and a stable anchor keeps that key stable when the heading’s words change.

Project hygiene

Rule Finds
engine a .qmd with constructs but no engine: knitr in its own front matter
above-setup a construct above the chunk that calls weft_setup()
dict-key dict$key for a key the dictionary does not hold
dict-assign chunk code that assigns to dict
tar-name tar_read() of a target the store does not hold
tar-cache a chunk that reads a target and has cache: true
file-link a link or image to a file that is not there
config-place a weft: key in _quarto.yml, or a project setting in a document
read a file that is not UTF-8

Python, Julia and Observable

A document that mixes languages reaches prose through R. These rules find the ways a value from another language goes wrong on the way.

Rule Tier Finds
guest-inline 1 inline code in another language, such as `{python} depth`, in a document knitr knits: knitr does not run it, so it prints as code
guest-call 1 r.fmt_num( and the like in a Python chunk, which pass arguments through reticulate and can turn a Python integer into a wrong number; from weft import fmt_num is safe
guest-read 2 py$n in R chunk code, and py_eval(), py_call(), julia_eval() and the like in a value, which weft does not check; py_value() and jl_value() are the guarded reads
ojs-value 2 an inline `{ojs} total` or a ${total} in an Observable md or html template, which the reader’s browser computes after weft’s checks have run

The first two block a commit like any tier-1 finding. The engine rule also says which engine Quarto would pick for a Python or Julia document and what to write instead.

Tier-2 heuristics

The tier-2 rules guess. Their findings are worth a look and never block anything:

  • claim-word: a quantifier, extreme or direction word (“all”, “only”, “largest”, “rose”) in a sentence with a value, which the value may no longer bear out, or in a new sentence with no value at all. A word inside an if or sign span is already guarded and is not listed.
  • if-zero: an if condition that compares with zero.
  • lone-bar: a bracket with one | and no governor, which is probably a span with a misspelt key.
  • name: a class or key that weft does not know, especially one that is one edit from a weft name, such as iff.
  • long-guard: an if arm longer than guard_words (25 words).
  • anchor-unused, xref-code: an anchor nobody refers to, and a cross-reference written inside a code span.

Over a whole project the tier-2 rules can list a great deal. They are meant for new material: changes() and verify() run them over the lines added since a commit.

Settings

Setting Default Governs
label_words [] words after which a number is exempt
numeral_years false whether a four-digit year is exempt
claim_words {add: [], drop: []} words added to or dropped from the claim-word list
claim_cap 20 claim-word sentences listed per file before a count replaces them
guard_words 25 the length of an if arm that long-guard lists
expected_names [] classes (.foo) and keys (foo) from other tools that name should accept
strict [] tier-1 rules whose every instance fails verify()

strict is for the end of adoption. Once a project has removed every typed number, strict: [numeral] makes verify() fail on any that remain, whether or not they were committed before.

The two readers

By default the lints tell prose from code with weft’s own reader, which runs no Pandoc and gives the same answer on every machine. lints(reader = "pandoc") also parses each document with Pandoc 3.0 or later, and counts a character as prose only when both readers agree. It finds the Pandoc version from the option weft.pandoc, the variable WEFT_PANDOC, Quarto, rmarkdown or the path.
